And.text: One of the 48 constellations catalogued by Ptolemy in the Almagest (Alexandria, about 150 AD), inherited from Greek tradition; the Greeks in turn drew many figures from Babylonian star lists such as MUL.APIN (about 1000 BC). The myths attached to it were gathered by Eratosthenes and Hyginus. Its modern boundaries were fixed by the IAU in 1930.

Car.text: Part of Argo Navis, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations. Argo was so large that Lacaille divided it in 1763 into the Keel (Carina), the Stern (Puppis), and the Sails (Vela); the IAU confirmed the split in 1930, so Argo itself no longer exists.

It is the only constellation named for a real person that survives in the modern list. Modern boundaries fixed by the IAU in 1930.

Cam.text: Introduced by the Dutch cartographer Petrus Plancius on a celestial globe of 1612 to fill the empty region near the pole; popularized by Jakob Bartsch's 1624 atlas. Modern boundaries fixed by the IAU in 1930.

Col.text: Separated from Canis Major by Petrus Plancius on a 1592 star map and named for the dove Noah released from the Ark. Modern boundaries fixed by the IAU in 1930.

Mon.text: Introduced by Petrus Plancius on his 1612 globe to fill the faint space between Orion and Canis Minor. Modern boundaries fixed by the IAU in 1930.

Cru.text: Its stars were known to the Greeks as part of Centaurus but slipped below the Mediterranean horizon through precession. European navigators of the 1500s rediscovered them; Plancius drew the Cross separately in 1598 and Augustin Royer formalized it in 1679. Modern boundaries fixed by the IAU in 1930.

Com.text: Known in antiquity as the tuft of hair at the tip of Leo's tail, and named by the court astronomer Conon in 245 BC for Queen Berenice II of Egypt. It became a constellation in its own right in Tycho Brahe's star catalogue of 1602. Modern boundaries fixed by the IAU in 1930.
